thread.title: Spotify’s No Lightweight – Barron’s – Breaking News

title: Spotify’s No Lightweight – Barron’s – Breaking News
text:
obunike 0 Comments Barrons , Lightweight , Spotifys Spread the love 
Spotify Technology (SPOT) made its market debut last week, using a unique method to sell shares that ostensibly cut out those meddling middlemen—investment bankers. There were fewer theatrics—no bankers forcing hoodie-wearing tech CEOs to talk to the suits. (Don’t worry, they still hired bankers, just not as many.) And the Swedish streaming music company didn’t sell any “new” shares; it just started allowing existing shareholders to offer theirs on the New York Stock Exchange. 
This led to some odd dynamics—notably, just 5% of the potentially available shares were traded at the opening price, a small number for a market debut, according to Bloomberg. A dearth of shares probably propped up the opening price. Spotify opened at $165.90, rose in the first few minutes, and then began a gradual slide that saw it end the day at $149.01. That’s either a 10% decline from the open or a 13% rise from the “reference price” that the NYSE had chosen as a kind of placeholder for traders. Overall, it was a remarkably bullish debut for a company whose last private valuation was from a share swap in December that valued the company at about 30% less. 
Launched in 2008, Spotify has arguably saved the music industry, or at least the record labels that rule it. Spotify’s growth—to 159 million monthly users, including 71 million paying “premium” subscribers, as of the end of 2017—was a boon for recording artists, who had been languishing in the post-CD, post-Napster world. After falling for 15 years starting in 1999, revenue for the industry grew in both 2015 and 2016, largely because of streaming subscriptions, which made up about a third of the $16 billion market as of 2016. 
Helping Axl Rose make another buck off “November Rain” doesn’t pay the bills, however. The service loses money, and has been doing so at an accelerating rate. Its biggest rival is the largest gorilla in the jungle, Apple (AAPL). And Spotify’s path to profitability depends on negotiations with a handful of big record labels, owned by Sony (SNE), Vivendi (VIVHY), and Time Warner (TWX) that control the bulk of global music rights. 
Spotify had $4.9 billion in revenue in 2017 (at current euro-to-dollar exchange rates) and expects about $6 billion this year. At its recent stock price of $146, the market is valuing the company at $26 billion. 
We’ve seen this dynamic before—a money-losing tech company popular with millennials trading at a seemingly unsustainable sky-high valuation. But Spotify isn’t Snap (SNAP). It’s one of the few must-have apps on your smartphone, and it’s likely to remain that way. Spotify has nearly twice the market share in paid subscribers of its closest competitor Apple, and many multiples more than Amazon.com (AMZN) and Alphabet (GOOGL), according to Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris. 
Not every tech company that butts heads with the tech behemoths loses. Grubhub (GRUB) is the market leader in mobile food ordering and is likely to stay that way, despite a similar list of competitors, for instance. Spotify, too, should be able to outpace Apple, in part because its unique service—curated playlists—has become more popular in the past few years, with 31% of listening on provided playlists last year, compared with less than 20% two years ago, Morris says. 
Smart tech and an artist-friendly reputation give Spotify an elusive quality that teenagers have sought for centuries: It’s cool, baby! “While the cool factor on its own may not seem to provide a deep moat, we believe it is a significant contributing factor in attracting and retaining talent and audience in an industry that itself is the epitome of cool,” Morris writes. 
Of course, no one buys a stock to be cool (or we hope they don’t), and Spotify’s valuation is lofty. But the company is trading at just four times the $6.4 billion in sales that Wall Street’s forecasts for it this year. That’s well within the range of other tech stocks. In fact, Grubhub trades for nine times its expected sales over the next 12 months, Netflix (NFLX) goes for above eight, and Google parent Alphabet fetches almost six. 
Of course, those other companies are profitable. Spotify still must cross that Rubicon. Spotify’s “growth mode” expenses for marketing and research are likely to keep it in the red for at least another year. The company expects operating losses of $283 million to $405 million this year, which would be a smaller deficit than last year. Spotify’s biggest cost—the rights to play music—remains subject to negotiation with those formidable record labels. But Spotify already appears to have had success in winning more profitable terms, Morris notes. Its gross margin—revenue net of content costs—rose to 21% in 2017 from 14% in 2016. This year, the company sees it hitting 23% to 25%. The record labels have incentives to keep Spotify healthy, because they hold significant stakes in the company, with Sony owning 5.7% (Sony sold 17% of its stake in the offering). Without Spotify, who will be on the other side of the negotiating table? Apple. And they’re no fun. 
Spotify’s stock price could remain volatile in the months ahead. It’s not clear whether more insiders will eventually sell stock, or whether Spotify will need to raise money in a more traditional equity offering. But betting on the stock now could do more than just show your kids how “with it” you are. Spotify’s stock could reasonably rise to five times sales, putting its valuation in line with the average analysts’ rating of $177. 
Streaming music—unlike the eight-track–isn’t going anywhere soon, and Spotify’s worth adding to the playlist.
